issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the dataset as a national probability/general-population sample, but the Methods describe a small university participant-pool sample of young students. This is a fundamental contradiction that makes it unclear what sample was actually analyzed and raises the possibility that different sections were copied from different studies.
issues.quote: "We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years." ... "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington." ... "Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1"

issues.description: Even taking the Methods at face value, a convenience sample from an introductory psychology pool with mean age 19 is not nationally representative or a probability sample. Claims of high generalizability to the New Zealand population are therefore unsupported.
issues.quote: "We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington." ... "Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population."

issues.subcategory: reported fit indices and confidence intervals incompatible with stated sample size
issues.description: Several reported statistics are mathematically inconsistent with the stated N=374. With χ²(2279)=36511.73 and N=374, RMSEA would be approximately .20, not .03. Likewise, the very narrow confidence intervals around means/correlations imply a sample in the thousands, not 374. This strongly suggests either the sample size, model-fit values, or descriptive statistics come from a different dataset or were reported incorrectly.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study" ... "Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07)" ... "Mean | 2.60 [2.58, 2.63]"

issues.description: The focal outcome is described inconsistently as willingness to change behaviour, willingness to sacrifice, and environmental concern. The items shown measure concern/exaggeration, not willingness to sacrifice or behavior change. These are distinct constructs, so the main dependent variable is not clearly defined or validly operationalized.
issues.quote: "people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment" ... "Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, \"How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?\" and \"To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?\"" ... "willingness to make sacrifices for the environment"

issues.description: The analysis is described as a path analysis on three variables, but the Methods then refer to item-level residual variances across time, implying a latent-variable longitudinal SEM. The paper does not clearly state whether constructs were modeled as observed scale scores or latent variables, nor how items were loaded, reverse-scored, or linked over time. This ambiguity prevents proper evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: "We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model included three variables across five measurement points" ... "We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points."

issues.description: Longitudinal comparisons require evidence that the constructs were measured comparably across waves. Instead, one RWA item was missing at Time 2, and the paper reports only equality constraints on residual variances, not tests of configural/metric/scalar invariance. Without invariance evidence, changes and cross-lagged effects may reflect measurement changes rather than construct change.
issues.quote: "The item \"Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the \"normal way\" things are supposed to be done\", was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points." ... "We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time"

issues.description: Using listwise deletion in a five-wave longitudinal study can substantially reduce the effective sample and bias estimates unless data are missing completely at random. The manuscript gives no justification for this choice and no sensitivity analysis comparing it with FIML or multiple imputation.
issues.quote: "Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion."

issues.subcategory: attrition and retention not reported in manuscript
issues.description: Key information needed to evaluate selection bias and representativeness across waves is omitted from the paper and deferred to an external website. Readers cannot assess dropout, wave-specific Ns, or whether the analyzed participants differ from those lost to follow-up.
issues.quote: "Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website."

issues.description: All cross-lagged parameters were constrained to be identical across waves because the authors were interested in an overall effect. However, the paper does not report testing whether these equality constraints were empirically justified. If effects vary across intervals, imposing stationarity can distort parameter estimates and substantive conclusions.
issues.quote: "We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant." ... "We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured."

issues.subcategory: invalid comparison of dependent correlations via non-overlapping CIs
issues.description: The manuscript treats non-overlapping confidence intervals as evidence that one zero-order correlation is stronger than another. This is not a valid test when the correlations are estimated in the same sample and share a variable; a formal test for dependent correlations is required.
issues.quote: "Of note here is that the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval."

issues.subcategory: claims stronger predictor despite non-significant difference test
issues.description: The manuscript reports that constraining the SDO→environment and RWA→environment paths to equality did not significantly worsen fit (p=.126), which means the data do not support a reliable difference between those paths. Despite this, the authors still interpret SDO as the stronger predictor and later describe it as significantly stronger. This is a direct inferential error that affects the main conclusion.
issues.quote: "We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample." ... "In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA."

issues.description: The Methods state that standardized parameters will be presented, but the figure caption says the figure reports unstandardized parameters, and the text reports B values without clarifying scale. This inconsistency makes it unclear what coefficients are actually being interpreted and compared.
issues.quote: "We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances." ... "Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL)."

issues.description: The paper states one significance threshold in the Methods and a different one in the figure caption. This suggests either inconsistent decision rules or inaccurate reporting.
issues.quote: "Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings." ... "All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted."

issues.subcategory: standard deviation reported instead of standard error for path estimates
issues.description: The coefficient summaries report B alongside "SD" rather than standard error. For model coefficients, uncertainty should be reported as SE. If "SD" is literal, the inferential statistics are uninterpretable; if SE was intended, the reporting is incorrect and confusing.
issues.quote: "SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01])."

issues.description: The reported χ² difference of 15,389.13 on 1 df is implausible given the tiny parameter estimates and the stated N=374. This strongly suggests a typographical or computational error and undermines confidence in the reported model-comparison tests.
issues.quote: "These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)"

issues.subcategory: causal claims from observational cross-lagged data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly interprets longitudinal associations as demonstrating causal influence. Cross-lagged panel models applied to observational survey data do not establish causality, especially without experimental manipulation or strong assumptions about confounding and measurement invariance.
issues.quote: "These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism." ... "This result indicates that the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future"

issues.description: The paper claims that the analyses disentangle directionality, but traditional cross-lagged models do not separate stable between-person differences from within-person changes and remain vulnerable to omitted-variable bias. The authors themselves later acknowledge that a third variable could explain both constructs, which directly weakens the claimed directional inference.
issues.quote: "These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships" ... "a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable."

issues.description: The manuscript attributes a combined SDO-RWA model to social dominance theory. However, RWA is not a component of Sidanius and Pratto’s social dominance theory; the joint treatment of SDO and RWA as separate but related ideological predictors is more closely associated with Duckitt’s dual-process model. This confuses the theoretical basis of the study.
issues.quote: "Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] social dominance theory proposes that SDO and RWA are separate but interrelated, and together predict attitudes towards different social groups."

issues.description: The manuscript infers specific motives—desire for dominance, submission to authority, tradition—from broad ideological scales, and further talks about motivation to exploit the environment even though the operationalized outcome is unclear and apparently not exploitation. These mechanistic claims are not directly tested by the data.
issues.quote: "These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority."

issues.description: The described sample is young, disproportionately female, and overwhelmingly Pākehā. Even apart from the convenience-sampling problem, these characteristics substantially limit external validity and make extrapolation to the New Zealand population inappropriate.
issues.quote: "Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European)."

issues.subcategory: unclear wave spacing and study duration
issues.description: The timing of the repeated measures is not clearly specified. "Five semesters" from 2009 to 2013 does not unambiguously indicate whether lags were annual, semiannual, or uneven. Cross-lagged effects are interpretable only relative to clearly defined lag intervals.
issues.quote: "This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)."

issues.subcategory: analysis materials unavailable during review and no preregistration reported
issues.description: The paper states that the Mplus syntax will only be made available upon acceptance, and it does not mention preregistration or a pre-specified analysis plan. Given the many modeling choices in longitudinal SEM, this leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom opaque during review.
issues.quote: "A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript."

issues.description: The manuscript justifies using p<.05 because of the 'large sample size,' but alpha thresholds are not chosen on that basis. Moreover, this rationale is especially odd given the stated N=374. The statement reflects confusion about inference and emphasizes p-values over effect-size interpretation.
issues.quote: "Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings."

issues.description: The discussion interprets an asymmetric cross-lag between RWA and SDO as evidence that New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism more than social dominance. The study contains no direct measures of socialization processes, and the inference goes well beyond what the model can support.
issues.quote: "Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance."
